terms.comment: The caterer’s promise in Martial: say how many you will be and what you will spend, “and dinner is ready for you”. For the other meals, jentāculum parātum est, prandium parātum est. Of food set on the table, appōnere (see “serve”): Cicero wrote one letter appositā secundā mēnsā, when dessert had been served.

evidence: Plaut. Stich. 662: namque edepol cēna cocta est
Plaut. Cas. 766: cēnam jam esse coctam oportuit
terms.comment: The kitchen’s word in Plautus: the food is cooked and can come to the table.

phrases.latin: dīc quotus et quantī cupiās cēnāre, nec ūnum addiderīs verbum: cēna parāta tibi est
phrases.english: say how many you will be at dinner and what you want to spend, and don’t add a word: your dinner is ready

phrases.latin: intrō abī et cēnam coque. properā. — Quīn tū īs accubitum, et convīvās cedo, corrumpitur jam cēna.
phrases.english: Go in and cook the dinner. Hurry. — Why don’t you go and take your place at table, and bring on the guests? The dinner is spoiling already.

phrases.latin: haec ad tē scrīpsī appositā secundā mēnsā
phrases.english: I wrote this to you when dessert had been served

phrases.latin: Cēna parāta est! Lavā manūs, venī.
phrases.english: Dinner’s ready! Wash your hands and come.

sources: Lewis & Short: cena · Lewis & Short: paro · Lewis & Short: coquo · Lewis & Short: appono
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 36.
